title: Electric Charge and Current of Electricity: Fundamental Concepts
topic: Electric Charge and Current of Electricity
subject: Combined Science (Physics)

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes electric charge?
options: There are three types of charge: positive, negative and neutral
Unlike charges attract and like charges repel
Charge can be created or destroyed in a circuit
questions.explanation: There are two types of electric charge: positive and negative. Unlike charges attract each other, while like charges repel. Charge is measured in coulombs (C).

questions.question: What is the unit of electric current?
questions.explanation: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge and is measured in amperes (A). 1 A = 1 C/s.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes between conventional current and electron flow?
options: Conventional current flows from negative to positive; electrons flow from positive to negative
Conventional current flows from positive to negative; electrons flow from negative to positive
Both conventional current and electron flow are in the same direction
Conventional current only exists in AC circuits
questions.explanation: Conventional current direction (established before electrons were discovered) is from positive to negative terminal. Electron flow is opposite: negative to positive.

questions.question: A charge of 120 C passes through a wire in 30 seconds. What is the current in the wire?
questions.explanation: Using Q = It, rearrange to I = Q/t. I = 120 C ÷ 30 s = 4 A.

questions.question: What does the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a cell represent?
options: The maximum current the cell can supply
The work done per unit charge by the source in driving charges around a complete circuit
The potential difference across the cell when no current flows
questions.explanation: E.m.f. is the work done per unit charge by the source in driving charges around a complete circuit. It is measured in volts (V).

questions.question: What is the potential difference across a component if 24 J of work is done to move 6 C of charge through it?
questions.explanation: Using V = W/Q: V = 24 J ÷ 6 C = 4 V. Potential difference is the work done per unit charge.

questions.question: Which statement correctly defines resistance?
questions.explanation: Resistance is defined as the ratio of potential difference to current: R = V/I. It is measured in ohms (Ω).

questions.question: A resistor has a potential difference of 9 V across it and a current of 3 A flowing through it. What is its resistance?
questions.explanation: Using R = V/I: R = 9 V ÷ 3 A = 3 Ω.

questions.question: Which factor does NOT affect the resistance of a wire?
questions.explanation: Resistance depends on length (R ∝ L), cross-sectional area (R ∝ 1/A), and material (resistivity). The current flowing through does not affect the resistance itself.

questions.question: A copper wire has resistance R. If its length is doubled while keeping the same thickness, what is the new resistance?
questions.explanation: Resistance is directly proportional to length (R ∝ L). Doubling the length doubles the resistance.

questions.question: A copper wire has resistance R. If its cross-sectional area is doubled while keeping the same length, what is the new resistance?
questions.explanation: Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (R ∝ 1/A). Doubling the area halves the resistance.

questions.question: What happens to the resistance of a metallic conductor when its temperature increases?
questions.explanation: For metallic conductors, resistance increases with temperature because the metal ions vibrate more vigorously, causing more collisions with electrons.

questions.question: Which graph represents a metallic conductor with fixed resistance at constant temperature?
options: A curved line through the origin
A straight line through the origin
questions.explanation: For a metallic conductor with fixed resistance at constant temperature, V ∝ I, so the I-V graph is a straight line through the origin with constant gradient.

questions.question: How should an ammeter be connected in a circuit to measure current?
questions.explanation: Ammeters measure current flowing through a point and must be connected in series so the same current flows through the meter.

questions.question: How should a voltmeter be connected to measure potential difference across a component?
questions.explanation: Voltmeters measure potential difference between two points and must be connected in parallel across the component.
